sources.title: Acute liver injury due to flavocoxid (Limbrel), a medical food for osteoarthritis: a case series
sources.authors: Chalasani N; Vuppalanchi R; Navarro V; Fontana R; Bonkovsky H; Barnhart H; Kleiner DE; Hoofnagle JH
quotes: Among 877 patients enrolled in the DILIN Prospective Study, 4 were attributed to flavocoxid.
All recovered uneventfully with no evidence acute liver failure or chronic liver injury.
Flavocoxid can cause significant liver injury which appears to resolve within weeks after its cessation.
The primary ingredients of flavocoxid are baicalin and catechins which are concentrated and standardized to greater than 90% purity.

Baicalin is a free-B ring flavonoid derived from the root of _Scutellaria baicalensis_ (Chinese skullcap), and multiple _in-vitro_ and animal experiments showed its hepatoprotective activity against a variety of hepatotoxic insults
sources.notes: DILIN prospective case series; full text fetched from PMC (abstract saved separately).

sources.title: Flavocoxid [LiverTox: Clinical and Research Information on Drug-Induced Liver Injury]
sources.authors: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
sources.journal_or_publisher: NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine
quotes: In premarketing clinical trials, serum aminotransferase elevations occurred in up to 10% of patients on flavocoxid therapy, but elevations above 3 times the upper limit of normal occurred in only 1% to 2% of recipients.
The time to onset was 1 to 5 months, and the pattern of enzyme elevations was usually hepatocellular or mixed.
Most cases were moderate in severity and no instance of acute liver failure or death has been reported.
this approval was withdrawn in December 2017 and it is not longer available as an FDA approved medical food.
The typical dose was 500 mg twice daily.
sources.notes: LiverTox monograph; likelihood score C (probable rare cause).

sources.title: Skullcap [LiverTox: Clinical and Research Information on Drug-Induced Liver Injury]
sources.authors: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
sources.journal_or_publisher: NCBI Bookshelf, National Library of Medicine
quotes: Skullcap has been implicated in rare instances of clinically apparent liver injury, although in most cases multiple herbal medications were being taken and the role of skullcap in the hepatic damage was unclear.
in some instances phytochemical analysis has identified significant adulterants (germander) or mislabeling in cases of suspected skullcap hepatotoxicity.
Recovery was rapid once the herbal was discontinued, but some cases have resulted in acute liver failure.
Chinese skullcap is a different species, but may also have adverse effects on the liver.

There have been several reports and small case series of acute liver injury with jaundice arising after 1 to 3 months of starting herbals or dietary supplements with Chinese skullcap (Scutellaria baicalensis), the liver injury resembling that associated with North American skullcap (Scutellaria lateriflora).
The authors review the literature on hepatotoxicity of Scutellaria baicalensis \[Chinese skullcap\] and conclude that there is no convincing evidence that it causes liver injury).

51 year old man developed abdominal pain followed by jaundice 10 days after starting a herbal supplement that contained Scutellariae baicalensis \[400 mg\] \[bilirubin 2.6 rising to 24.0 mg/dL, ALT 147 U/L, Alk P 147 U/L, INR 1.0\], worsening for 3 weeks but then resolving within 12 weeks of stopping).
Two patients developed liver injury within weeks of taking “Move Free Advanced”, which contains Chinese skullcap \[Scutellaria baicalensis\] for arthralgias, resolving upon stopping).
there is no obvious adverse reaction in the oral preparation of Scutellaria baicalensis”, but it may cause stomach discomfort, diarrhea and other minor symptoms in some patients).
sources.notes: LiverTox monograph distinguishing American and Chinese skullcap; annotated bibliography carries case-level details for Braude, Linnebur and Puri reports.

claims.quote: Baicalein showed an inhibitory effect on the activity of CYP3A4 with the IC50 value of 12.03 μM, which is responsible for the metabolism of simvastatin.

claims.claim: Baicalin exhibits antiplatelet, anticoagulant, and profibrinolytic activities, inhibiting thrombin-catalyzed fibrin polymerization, platelet function, and thrombin/FXa activities, and prolonging in vivo bleeding time in mice.
claims.quote: Our data showed that baicalin inhibited thrombin-catalyzed fibrin polymerization and platelet functions, prolonged aPTT and PT significantly and inhibited the activities and production of thrombin and FXa.

claims.claim: Wogonin inhibits human MAO-A and MAO-B in vitro (IC50 6.35 and 20.8 uM, respectively) while baicalein selectively and moderately inhibits MAO-A — in vitro enzymology with no clinical MAO-inhibitor-type interaction data.
claims.quote: Wogonin (11) effectively inhibited MAO-A and MAO-B (IC50=6.35 and 20.8μM, respectively).

claims.claim: Baicalein significantly reduces blood glucose in alloxan-diabetic rats, warranting awareness of potential hypoglycemic additivity with antidiabetic drugs despite the absence of clinical reports.
claims.quote: TXN and BCN significantly reduced blood glucose levels, improved lipid profiles, and decreased oxidative stress in diabetic rats.

claims.claim: Classic developmental-toxicity studies found a significant dose-dependent increase in fetal skeletal variations (lumbar rib) in rats given Scutellariae Radix water extract during organogenesis, although follow-up work characterized the lumbar rib as a transient fetal variation at 100-fold typical human intake.
claims.quote: There was a significant (P < 0.05) dose-dependent increase in the incidence of skeletal variations (presence of lumbar rib).

claims.claim: A UPLC-MS/MS survey of 386 Chinese Pharmacopoeia herbal medicines detected pyrrolizidine alkaloids in 271 samples (0.1-25,567.4 ug/kg), with 20 samples above the 0.007 ug/kg bw/day baseline and 10 with lifetime MOE below 10,000.
claims.quote: Results showed that PAs was detected in 271 out of 386 samples with a content of 0.1–25,567.4 μg/kg, and there were 20 samples with EDI values above the baseline, 0.007 μg/kg bw/day.

claims.claim: Scutellaria barbata was among the PA-positive herbs in that survey (total PAs 61.7 ug/kg; EDI 0.026 ug/kg bw/day at the 30 g/day pharmacopoeial maximum; lifetime MOE 8,958; two-weeks-per-year MOE 232,918), whereas Scutellaria baicalensis is not among the herbs named in the publication.
